'''Ralph Palmer Agnew''' (December 29, 1900 – October 16, 1986)<ref name=":1" /> was an [[American people|American]] [[mathematician]]. His research concerned summability of [[Series (mathematics)|series]]; he also wrote textbooks on [[calculus]] and [[differential equation]]s.

== Biography ==
Agnew was born in [[Poland, Ohio]], and did his undergraduate studies at [[Allegheny College]]. After completing a master's degree at [[Iowa State College]] he moved to [[Cornell University]], where he received a Ph.D. in 1930. He was appointed to the Cornell faculty in 1931. He chaired the mathematics department at Cornell from 1940 to 1950, and was responsible for bringing [[William Feller]] and [[Mark Kac]] to Cornell.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=42748}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite web |url=https://ecommons.library.cornell.edu/bitstream/1813/19237/1/Agnew_Ralph_Palmer_1986.pdf |title=Ralph Palmer Agnew |last1=Livesay |first1=G. Roger |last2=Nerode |first2=Anil |author-link2=Anil Nerode |last3=Fuchs |first3=Wolfgang H. |author-link3=Wolfgang Heinrich Johannes Fuchs |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211009202314/https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/handle/1813/19237/Agnew_Ralph_Palmer_1986.pdf?sequence=1 |archive-date=2021-10-09 |url-status=live}}</ref> He died in 1986.<ref name=":1" />

== Research ==

=== Summability ===
In 1932, Agnew studied the notion of a "deferred Cesàro mean", which is a variant of a [[Cesàro summation|Cesàro mean]] in which the transformed sequence is of the form <math>D_n = \frac{s_{p_n + 1} + s_{p_n + 2} + \cdots + s_{q_n}}{q_n - p_n}</math>. In particular, he found that it was consistent with the Cesàro mean if the sequence <math>p_n/(q_n - p_n)</math> is bounded.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Agnew |first=Ralph Palmer |date=1932 |title=On Deferred Cesaro Means |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1968524 |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=413–421 |doi=10.2307/1968524 |issn=0003-486X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 1949, Agnew proved the following theorem relating the [[partial sums]] of a sequence to its [[Abel transform]]:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Agnew |first=Ralph Palmer |date=1949 |title=Abel Transforms and Partial Sums of Tauberian Series |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1969355 |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=50 |issue=1 |pages=110–117 |doi=10.2307/1969355 |issn=0003-486X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><math display="block">{\lim\sup}_{t\to 1^-}|\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} t^ku_k - \sum_{k=1}^{[q/\log t^{-1}]} u_k|\leq A(q)\lim\sup |nu_n|.</math>

=== Probability ===
In 1954, Agnew studied strengthening the [[central limit theorem]]. In particular, let <math>\xi_i</math> denotes [[independent and identically distributed]] random variables with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, let <math>F_n(x)</math> denote the [[cumulative distribution function]] (CDF) of the sum <math>\frac{\xi_1 + \cdots + \xi_n}{\sqrt{n}}</math>, and let <math>\Phi(x)</math> denote the [[standard normal CDF]]. Then the central limit theorem says that <math>F_n(x)\to\Phi(x)</math> for all values of ''x''; Agnew proved the stronger result that the integral <math>\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |F_n(x) - \Phi(x)|^p dx</math> converges to zero for all values of ''p'' greater than one half.<ref>{{Cite web |title=GLOBAL VERSIONS OF THE CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM* |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.40.9.800 |access-date=2025-12-04 |website=www.pnas.org |language=en |doi=10.1073/pnas.40.9.800 |pmc=534170 |pmid=16589563}}</ref> In 1956, he went on to estimate this integral when ''p'' = 2 in the case of the [[symmetric binomial distribution]] (where each term is +1 or -1 with equal probability) and in the case of each term following a [[continuous uniform distribution]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Agnew |first=Ralph Palmer |date=March 1957 |title=Estimates for Global Central Limit Theorems |url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aoms/1177707035 |journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics |language=en |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=26–42 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177707035 |issn=0003-4851}}</ref> In the former case, the integral is on the order of <math>1/n</math>; in the latter case, it converges faster, on the order of <math>1/n^2</math>.<ref name=":0" />

== Textbooks ==
One well-known example for dealing with a system of elementary differential equations attributed to Agnew is the "snow plow problem", which is stated as:<ref>{{cite web |title=Snow plow problem |url=http://sites.science.oregonstate.edu/~show/docs/256-SnowPlow.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201024201913/https://sites.science.oregonstate.edu/~show/docs/256-SnowPlow.pdf |archive-date=2020-10-24 |website=sites.science.oregonstate.edu |publisher=Oregon State University}}</ref>
<blockquote>
It starts snowing in the morning and continues heavily and steadily throughout the day. A snow-plow starts plowing at noon and plows 2 miles in the first hour, and 1 mile in the second. What time did it start snowing?
</blockquote>
The problem is deceptive for its paucity of information, and requires several common sense assumptions such as the instantaneous velocity of the plow is proportional to the depth of snow immediately in front of it, and there is no maximum or limiting velocity. These are arbitrary, but bear a particular relationship to each other. In the end, they cancel out of the equation and do not appear in the solution, which is a fixed time of day.<ref>''Differential Equations'', McGraw-Hill, 1942, pp. 30–32 (pp. 39-40 in the 1960, 2nd edition).</ref>

His textbook on differential equations also contains a rather humorous note on the difficulty of converting a Laplace equation directly from Rectangular (Cartesian) coordinates to Spherical coordinates:
<blockquote>Doing this can make you forget your troubles the next time you have a toothache at an airport and are informed that your plane is 3 hours late.<ref>''Differential Equations'', 2nd ed., McGraw-Hill, 1960, p. 148.</ref>
</blockquote>
